items.t: Munich Re Lifts Full-Year Outlook as Nine-Month Profit Climbs to €5.7 Billion
sum: Munich Re has raised its profit target for the current year, pointing to a light burden from major claims in its property-casualty reinsurance business as the driver behind the upgrade. The improved guidance lands alongside a softer third quarter, a combination that gives the group's full-year story two distinct halves.

For the first nine months of 2026, the reinsurer reported a group profit of €5.67 billion, up from €5.18 billion in the same period a year earlier. Insurance revenue for the nine-month stretch reached €46.6 billion.

The third quarter on its own told a different story. Group net profit came in at €1.74 billion, down from €2 billion in the prior-year quarter. Insurance revenue for the three months totaled €16.6 billion. According to Handelsblatt, both the quarterly revenue and the quarterly result beat analysts' expectations.

Alongside the quarterly release on Thursday, Munich Re set out its expectations for the full year 2026. In property-casualty reinsurance, it anticipates a combined ratio below 80%. For Global Specialty Insurance, it expects a figure under 90%. The company attributed the improved property-casualty expectation to the lower major-claim load.

Separately, Munich Re reported fresh purchases under its ongoing buyback program on Tuesday. Between October 30 and November 9 inclusive, the company acquired 115,000 of its own shares. Since the program began on May 14, repurchases had reached roughly 3.3 million shares through November 9, based on trades already executed as of that cut-off date.
The stock added 1.0% on the previous day, closing at €591.00, a gain that followed Thursday's publication of the quarterly statement.

items.t: Munich Re's Earnings Beat Runs Into Two Walls of Caution
Munich Re stock: Q3 profit falls as 2026 target rises
sum: Munich Re reported a lower third-quarter net result on Thursday, November 12, 2026, but raised its full-year profit target after a strong first nine months. The figures were published in the company's quarterly statement, carried by MarketScreener.

Munich Re generated a net result of 1.742 billion euros in the third quarter, down from 1.997 billion euros a year earlier. The comparison was affected by exceptionally low major-loss expenditure in the third quarter of 2025. Major losses after retrocession and before tax reached 646 million euros, compared with 118 million euros in the prior-year quarter, but remained below the 18% level expected by the company.

The broader nine-month result was stronger. Net income rose to 5.667 billion euros from 5.176 billion euros in the first nine months of 2025. Insurance revenue from insurance contracts issued increased to 16.626 billion euros in the third quarter from 14.575 billion euros and reached 46.583 billion euros for the first nine months, compared with 45.162 billion euros a year earlier.

Life and health reinsurance provided a notable contribution. Its third-quarter technical result increased to 493 million euros from 314 million euros, while the segment's net result rose to 340 million euros from 286 million euros. The company attributed the development to strong new business and favourable claims experience, particularly in mortality.

Property-casualty reinsurance produced a net result of 938 million euros, below the prior-year 1.187 billion euros. Its combined ratio was 80.0%, compared with 62.7% a year earlier. Global Specialty Insurance posted a combined ratio of 83.9%, while ERGO contributed 263 million euros to group net income.

Munich Re raised its 2026 net result target to 6.6 billion euros from 6.3 billion euros. The company now expects a net combined ratio below 80% for property-casualty reinsurance and below 90% for Global Specialty Insurance, improving both thresholds from approximately 80% and 90%, respectively. Other expectations in its half-year report remained unchanged.
The revised target leaves execution and claims experience as the main focus for investors through year-end.

Munich Re's Buyback and Raised Guidance Meet a Wall of Analyst Caution
sum: Munich Re has spent the past three weeks telling the market to expect more: a full-year 2026 net profit target lifted from €6.3 billion to €6.6 billion, a provisional third-quarter result of roughly €1.7 billion, and a nine-month tally of €5.7 billion. Now the market is asking whether that earnings strength can survive the renewal season.

The stock drew two very different verdicts from the analyst community within days of each other. On Friday, JPMorgan's Kamran Hossain cut his rating from "Overweight" to "Neutral" while keeping a €590 price target, citing expected pressure on reinsurance prices in the 2027 renewal round and a valuation he now considers adequate following the shares' strong run. The downgrade weighed on Munich Re and its reinsurance peers on Friday, according to dpa-AFX. The stock was up 1.8% at €576.80 on the day of the note, having gained 2.2% a day earlier.
Bankhaus Metzler took the opposite view on 4 November, reaffirming its "Buy" recommendation and raising its price target from €600 to €643.

Alongside the debate over pricing, Munich Re has been quietly shrinking its share count. The company reported buying back 115,000 of its own shares in the period from 30 October through 9 November inclusive — a reminder that management is returning capital even as the operating outlook comes under scrutiny.

The next hard data point arrives on 12 November 2026, when Munich Re publishes its final third-quarter results. Investors will be looking for two things at once: confirmation that the preliminary figures hold, and management commentary convincing enough to suggest the earnings base can withstand softer pricing at the upcoming renewals.

Governance news has added another thread to the story. Munich Re announced on 21 October that board member Clarisse Kopff would leave at the end of that month. Her position will not be filled permanently; Thomas Blunck takes on her responsibilities in addition to his own.

The gap between the two analyst houses comes down to how much weight each places on the renewal cycle. Hossain's concern is forward-looking — a pricing expectation rather than a reported fact, with the severity of any decline and its consequences for Munich Re still a matter of scenario-building.

sum: Munich Re shares closed Friday at €569.00, down 4.0%, after JPMorgan cut its rating on the reinsurer from "Overweight" to "Neutral" — a downgrade that landed alongside a fresh warning about pricing in the sector beyond 2027.

The US bank left its price target untouched at €590, a combination that suggests a more measured weighing of upside and risk rather than a wholesale reassessment of the company's value. JPMorgan analyst Kamran Hossain also downgraded Hannover Rück on the same day, moving that stock from "Neutral" to "Underweight," and both reinsurers came under pressure following the calls, according to dpa-AFX.

At the heart of JPMorgan's more cautious stance is the expectation of continued price pressure and possible margin compression in property and casualty reinsurance in 2027. That shifts the debate toward how much earning power Munich Re can hold onto if contract terms weaken in the next renewal round.

The timing matters. Munich Re raised its profit guidance roughly two weeks ago, lifting the 2026 target to €6.6 billion from €6.3 billion. Preliminary figures for the third quarter of 2026 put net profit at around €1.7 billion, while the nine-month group result came in at €5.7 billion. According to Reuters, lower-than-expected major claims and a strong investment result drove the solid quarter.

Those numbers give the bullish case something concrete to stand on — but they also invite scrutiny. A high profit level supports the stock more firmly the more durable its foundations look under changed market conditions. If contract terms deteriorate, a positive view would have to rest more heavily on the rest of the earnings picture.

For the optimistic scenario to hold, the final publication would need to confirm the operating strength already flagged and, just as importantly, give investors confidence in its staying power. Lower major claims and a strong investment result explain the recent run — but a longer-term positive assessment would require convincing evidence of profitability even when those tailwinds fade.
Should the company's commentary point to declining profitability — particularly a combination of softer prices and weakening support from those same earnings drivers — the bearish case gains weight.

sum: Munich Re's stock fell 4.0% on Friday, caught in a broader pullback across the European insurance sector, after JPMorgan downgraded the German reinsurer from "Overweight" to "Neutral." The broker left its price target unchanged at EUR 590.

The downgrade landed alongside a wider flight from riskier assets that weighed on insurers globally, according to Reuters. The European insurance sector shed 2.6% on the day. JPMorgan's move also hit Hannover Rück, with dpa-AFX reporting that both reinsurers came under pressure following the broker's decisions.

At the heart of JPMorgan's caution is expected pricing pressure in the 2027 renewal round. Analyst Kamran Hossain pointed to a comparatively benign 2026 hurricane season as a key factor behind the softer outlook for reinsurance contracts covering the coming year. The broker sees margin compression looming, particularly in property-casualty reinsurance, and views the stock's further upside as limited.

The downgrade comes despite a strong run of company news from Munich Re. Roughly two weeks ago the group raised its 2026 net profit guidance to EUR 6.6 billion from EUR 6.3 billion, and reported a preliminary third-quarter net profit of about EUR 1.7 billion. For the first nine months of the year, group earnings reached EUR 5.7 billion.

Alongside the improved outlook, Munich Re has been returning capital to shareholders. In a disclosure made about three weeks ago, the company reported buying back 97,500 of its own shares during the period covered. Since the programme began, roughly 3.2 million shares had been repurchased by the end of that reporting window.

The group's management board is also set to shrink. Reuters reported about three weeks ago that Clarisse Kopff would leave the company at the end of October, with her board position to remain permanently vacant. Thomas Blunck is to take on her responsibilities in addition to his own, reducing the board from eleven members to ten from November.
Investors will get the full picture on 12 November, when Munich Re publishes its detailed quarterly results. According to the company calendar, the release is scheduled for around 7:30 a.m. CET.

Munich Re's Upgraded Outlook Meets JPMorgan's Cautious Turn on 2027 Renewals
sum: Munich Re has spent the past fortnight telling investors to expect more, not less: a preliminary net profit of roughly EUR 1.7 billion for the third quarter of 2026, a nine-month tally of EUR 5.7 billion, and a full-year guidance lifted to EUR 6.6 billion from EUR 6.3 billion. JPMorgan, however, has chosen this moment to step back from the stock.

The US bank cut its rating to "Neutral" from "Overweight," with analyst Kamran Hossain pointing to anticipated pricing pressure at the 2027 renewal round and a total return that now looks less compelling against primary insurers following the shares' strong run. The price target was left untouched at EUR 590 — a recommendation downgrade without a corresponding trim to the valuation mark.

Shares fell 4.0% in the session following the move. dpa-AFX attributed the decline to the JPMorgan downgrade and a weak broader market acting in tandem, while Reuters reported a simultaneous slide across the European insurance sector. The soft backdrop amplified the headwind, though the more consequential question for investors is how durable the pricing assumptions for the coming renewal season will prove.

Hossain's case ties operational risk to relative valuation. A stock can lose appeal when rival insurers offer a more favorable balance of reward and risk, and Munich Re must now persuade shareholders on both fronts — its own underwriting trajectory and its standing against primary carriers.

The constructive path requires pricing concessions to stay within economically viable bounds. Should Munich Re demonstrate that attractive terms remain achievable even under firmer pressure, fears of a sharp deterioration would look overstated — and the recent re-rating by JPMorgan would carry less weight. The key would be a convincing link between pricing trends and bottom-line results, giving investors a sturdier foundation than simply betting on a rebound after the drop. Evidence would need to come from the company itself and, later, from the actual course of the renewal round.

The bearish scenario starts with pricing pressure that is stronger or broader than currently expected. If Munich Re has to accept less favorable terms, expectations for future earnings power could suffer, lending Hossain's caution added force.

sum: JPMorgan has taken a more cautious view of Munich Re. On Friday, November 6, 2026, dpa-AFX reported that the US bank had cut its rating from Overweight to Neutral while keeping its price target at 590 euros. The report was based on an original study published on November 5.

Analyst Kamran Hossain said reinsurers had experienced their strongest period in three decades when measured by returns on equity. In his view, the next phase will be more difficult. JPMorgan expects further pricing pressure in the 2027 renewal round and considers Munich Re's current valuation appropriate.

The downgrade reflects a more selective assessment of future returns rather than a change to the price target. JPMorgan also argued that the total return outlook for reinsurers was no longer particularly attractive compared with primary insurers after the sector's strong run.

The backdrop is important for Munich Re because renewal pricing directly affects the profitability and volume of its reinsurance book. Lower prices can support client demand but may compress returns if underwriting discipline weakens. The company's approach to complex risks and selective capital deployment therefore remains central to the investment case.

sum: Munich Re's supervisory board has folded Clarisse Kopff's duties into Thomas Blunck's remit, a permanent reshuffle that took effect on Sunday and leaves one executive seat unfilled. The board approved the added responsibility on 21 October; Kopff left the management team on Saturday, and her position will not be filled on a lasting basis. Blunck now also oversees P&C Reinsurance Europe & Latin America.

The move lands weeks after the reinsurer raised its 2026 net profit guidance from €6.3bn to €6.6bn on 23 October. Investors therefore face a two-track story: a capital return programme already well documented, and a profit ambition that still rests on preliminary figures.

Munich Re reported the purchase of 97,500 of its own shares in a mandatory disclosure dated 30 October. The transactions ran from 21 through 29 October, bringing the cumulative volume bought back since the programme began on 14 May to 3,189,311 shares.
That builds on an earlier filing covering 14 to 20 October, when 45,000 shares were acquired. The latest notice simply extends the same programme beyond the window previously reported.

It is worth separating the two strands. A buyback is a capital measure; the profit guidance concerns expected earnings. They sit side by side without one implying anything about the other's future path.

The operational backdrop is the preview published on 23 October. Munich Re put provisional third-quarter 2026 net profit at roughly €1.7bn, citing a strong operating performance, below-average major-loss claims in property-casualty reinsurance, and a robust investment result. The improvement, by the company's own account, did not rest on claims experience alone.
Across the first nine months of 2026, net profit reached €5.7bn. That figure underpins the raised full-year target of €6.6bn.

sum: Munich Re is expanding on two fronts at once. Munich Re Specialty began writing primary insurance in Australia today, with a Sydney-based unit targeting mid-sized commercial clients, while a signed risk-sharing agreement with the Africa Finance Corporation will see the reinsurer take a slice of trade finance guarantees for African banks. Both moves land in the same week that a preliminary third-quarter profit of roughly €1.7 billion cleared the analyst consensus of €1.479 billion.

The Australian operation is not a pure distribution play. Contracts are underwritten by Great Lakes Insurance SE, and the local team holds binding authority, meaning the unit can take on insurance risk on the ground. The offering spans property, construction, engineering, mining and surety lines. Chris Mackinnon heads the business, with Chris Harnett, Angus Kench and Alison Percival covering underwriting, claims and partnerships respectively.

The addressable market is sizeable on paper. ANZ Research expects major project activity to hit a record $80.3 billion in the 2026 financial year, and Infrastructure Australia puts the construction pipeline at $1.14 trillion. Project volume alone, however, says nothing about underwriting profitability — particularly in construction and surety, where the financial health of the insured counterparty is central to the risk. ASIC data show that 27% of corporate insolvencies in the 2023/24 financial year came from the construction sector, involving 2,975 companies.

In Africa, the approach is different in structure. The Africa Finance Corporation disclosed on 26 October a signed $1 billion risk-sharing facility covering trade finance guarantees for African banks, designed to support lending to small businesses. Munich Re will automatically take a share of eligible AFC transactions, with the partner retaining part of the risk on each deal. As financings are repaid, capacity becomes available for further business. The programme is intended to help narrow Africa's estimated annual trade finance gap of $80–120 billion and to support trade under the AfCFTA free trade area.
Neither initiative comes with a demonstrated earnings contribution yet.

ZAWYA: Africa Finance Corporation, Munich Re sign $1bln risk sharing deal
sum: The Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) and Munich Re have signed a $1 billion agreement to provide trade finance guarantees to African banks in an effort to boost lending to small businesses in the continent under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCfTA) trade agreement.

This massive capital injection seeks to address Africa’s estimated annual trade finance gap of between $80 billion and $120 billion, offering a major boost to the continent’s 1.3 billion people free trade market.

AFC, the continent’s infrastructure solutions provider and Munich Re, one of the world’s leading providers of reinsurance, primary insurance and insurance-related risk solutions have agreed in sharing the financial risks to allow African banks lend money to small businesses in the continent.

In a statement dated October 26 AFC said the financing under the Unfunded Managed Debt Mobilisation Programme (UMDMP) provides committed risk-sharing support for its trade finance lending to African financial institutions, coming at a time when African banks are struggling for liquidity to finance intra-African and international trade flows that boost their domestic economiesFor decades, African banks have struggled to secure foreign currency and credit lines to support local businesses trading across borders. Perceived high risks have traditionally starved the continent of the liquidity required to make the AfCFTA a fully realised success.
By derisking trade transactions, the partnership is expected unlock vital capital, allowing local financial institutions to back cross-border commerce with confidence.

Under the risk-sharing deal Munich Re will take a share of eligible AFC transactions automatically, while AFC will retain a part of the risk on every transaction, keeping both institutions’ interests aligned.

As the transactions under the programme mature, the programme’s capacity is freed up and reused to finance new investments.“Across the development finance landscape, there is a growing recognition that the scale of Africa’s financing needs cannot be met through traditional balance sheet lending alone.

Munich Re's Buyback Keeps Rolling While the Street Splits on What the Stock Is Worth
sum: Munich Re has spent the past six months quietly shrinking its share count, and the latest regulatory filing shows no sign of a pause. Between 21 and 29 October the reinsurer repurchased 97,500 of its own shares, extending a programme that began on 14 May and has now accumulated 3,189,311 shares through 29 October. The disclosure, published on Friday, confirms execution of an existing authorisation rather than the launch of any fresh capital measure — a distinction that matters when reading the headline.
What the buyback does not do is settle the valuation debate. On that front, the brokerage community remains genuinely divided.

BNP Paribas Exane downgraded Munich Re on 26 October, moving from "Outperform" to "Neutral" while holding its price target at €580, according to media reports. The more cautious stance therefore came without any reduction in the target — a signal that the call was about relative appeal rather than a diminished view of intrinsic worth.

Barclays, by contrast, went the other way. Roughly two weeks earlier, the UK bank nudged its target from €593 to €594 and reaffirmed an "Overweight" rating, media reports indicated. Neither house lowered its target, yet the two arrived at opposite recommendations. For investors, the takeaway is that the improved earnings outlook has not translated automatically into a uniformly more favourable rating — what each analyst thinks the shares can still deliver is doing much of the work.

The numbers underpinning the more constructive case arrived about a week ago. Munich Re reported a preliminary third-quarter 2026 net profit of roughly €1.7 billion, taking the nine-month tally to €5.7 billion. Management attributed the result to operating momentum across all segments, below-average major-loss activity in property-casualty reinsurance, and a strong investment result. The company was explicit that the performance rested on several drivers rather than a single benign catastrophe load.
Alongside those figures came a raised profit target: net income for 2026 is now guided at €6.6 billion, up from €6.3 billion previously.
Preliminary figures are not final figures, and Munich Re has a separate date circled for the completed picture. Full third-quarter 2026 results are scheduled for release on 12 November.

items.t: Munich Re Q1 net profit jumps 57% on lighter major-loss burden
sum: Munich Re's first-quarter results showed a 57% jump in net profit to €1,714 million, with the reinsurance business lifted by a lighter major-loss burden as the group recovered from a year-ago period weighed down by the Los Angeles wildfires.
The figure came in roughly in line with the €1,729 million analyst consensus.

The total technical result climbed to €2,676 million from €2,054 million, while the operating result rose to €2,230 million from €1,465 million. Insurance revenue from contracts issued slipped to €15,018 million from €15,811 million on adverse currency translation.

The currency result improved to –€162 million from –€506 million, with the prior-year figure reflecting greater US dollar exposure and depreciation. The effective tax rate eased to 20.9% from 22.3%, and annualized return on equity rose to 19.7% from 13.3%.

Equity rose to €34,616 million from €33,421 million at year-end 2025. The Solvency II ratio stood at 292%, down from 298%, well above the group's >200% target, and already includes a planned €2.25 billion buyback flagged with the 2025 results.

The reinsurance field of business contributed €1,479 million to the net result. Property-casualty reinsurance posted a net result of €841 million, with the combined ratio improving to 66.8% from 83.9%; the normalized combined ratio was 80.3%.

Major-loss expenditure in P&C reinsurance fell sharply to €130 million from €1,008 million, equivalent to 3.5% of net insurance revenue versus an expected 18%. The prior-year quarter had been weighed down by the Los Angeles wildfires.

RenaissanceRe sees stronger reinsurance demand ahead of mid-year renewals
sum: RenaissanceRe is seeing stronger-than-expected demand for reinsurance protection ahead of the mid-year renewals, with new buying activity running above assumptions set at January 1.
David Marra, Group Chief Underwriting Officer at RenaissanceRe, said the market is creating good opportunities to deploy capital, especially across U.S. property catastrophe business.

The company has already bound about half of its U.S. mid-year portfolio. Around half of that volume was completed on private terms, giving the reinsurer early access to placements at conditions it views as better than open-market levels.
Florida remains a major focus. Marra said the market continues to benefit from strong pricing, reduced social inflation after tort reform, and firm terms and conditions.

Policies at Citizens have fallen to record lows, reflecting a shift from public-market risk absorption toward private-market capacity. That shift supports the wider distribution chain and increases demand for reinsurance.

RenRe expanded in Florida through its Validus acquisition and through organic growth in 2025. The group is well positioned to capture profitable business from existing programmes and new demand through Q2.

The wider property book remains actively managed. RenRe continues reducing peak exposure while protecting margins. The portfolio is performing well, supported by strong current-year and prior-year loss ratios. Terms and conditions remain solid, though pricing faces more pressure in some areas.

items.t: Munich Re taps Schubert to lead Capital Partners division
sum: Munich Re has appointed Leonie Schubert (pictured above) as global head of Capital Partners, signaling continuity in a division that has become central to the reinsurance giant's structured solutions and capital markets strategy.

Schubert assumed the role effective March 1, 2026, overseeing the unit's strategic development and international investment operations as the reinsurance market navigates heightened complexity around capital deployment.

Schubert will share leadership with August Proebstl through June 2026, when Proebstl is scheduled to retire. The six-month transition arrangement reflects Munich Re's effort to maintain stability in a business line that has grown increasingly significant to its operations.

Capital Partners is Munich Re's umbrella division for risk trading, insurance-linked securities, catastrophe bonds and retrocession activities. The unit operates global hubs in Munich and Zurich, with recent expansion into Asia-Pacific through offices in Singapore and Beijing.

The division has built considerable muscle in the ILS market. It originates, structures and analyzes both prospective and retroactive reinsurance solutions, while also functioning as an active capital market investor.

August Proebstl previously headed Munich Re's corporate insurance partner unit before taking the helm at Capital Partners.

items.t: Munich Re names Leonie Schubert as new Global Head of Capital Partners
sum: Global reinsurance giant Munich Re announced that Leonie Schubert has stepped into the role of Global Head of Capital Partners from March 1st, which sees her leading the division of the company where capital market solutions and investor partnerships are managed.

The Capital Partners unit at Munich Re was established to bring together clients needs beyond traditional insurance and reinsurance risk transfer solutions, bundling together structured prospective, retroactive and capital market based reinsurance offerings under one business and team.

Capital Partners also encompasses Munich Re’s activities in the insurance-linked securities (ILS) market, including in structuring deals such as catastrophe bonds, sidecars, ILW’s, risk swaps and derivatives, assisting investors in the space, and even in the past as an active buyer and investor itself.
Today, Munich Re stated, “We are pleased to announce that Leonie Schubert will assume the role as Global Head of Capital Partners as of 1 March 2026.

“From March to June 2026, Leonie will co-lead the Capital Partners unit together with August Proebstl ahead of his retirement. This joint leadership period ensures continuity, leverages complementary experience, and supports a seamless transition for our teams and business partners.”

The global reinsurance firm further explained, “Leonie brings a strong strategic mindset, deep market expertise, and a clear focus on long term value creation. Together with the Capital Partners leadership team, she will continue to advance the strategic development of the unit and further strengthen our position in the international investment and capital markets landscape.
“We thank all colleagues who have supported this transition and look forward to shaping the future of Munich Re Capital Partners together.”

items.t: Study: Severe hailstorms increasing most rapidly in Europe
sum: The frequency of severe hailstorms is increasing more rapidly in Europe than anywhere else in the world. Closely linked to climate change, such storms can cause considerable damage. This is a key takeaway from a recent study compiled by researchers from the European Severe Storms Laboratory (ESSL), the Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznań, and Munich Re, published in Nature Geoscience, a science journal1. The researchers analysed weather data from 1950 to 2023 and insurance losses from 1992 to 2023.

Referred to as very large hail (or VLH), hailstones larger than 5 centimetres can cause considerable damage to buildings, vehicles and infrastructure – and also pose a danger to people. When severe hailstorms strike densely populated areas, losses quickly run into the billions. The study in Nature Geoscience analysed the correlations between weather data, the frequency of VLH, and loss trends. Small hail (< 2 cm) can also cause significant damage, especially in agriculture.

This study is the first comprehensive analysis of global risks, trends and losses with regard to very large hail. Its insights have enabled us to enhance our hail risk model for Europe, which now reflects cutting-edge research. In short, it's a tremendous boon to our specialists in risk assessment and underwriting.
Mean trend in annual number of VLH events per decade between 1950 and 2023
In the United States, the hail hazard varied. While no increase was observed in many regions, the risk of very large hailstones rose by around 50% in and near Dallas, Texas, for example.

By contrast, the frequency of VLH decreased significantly in some parts of the southern hemisphere, particularly in South America. The study’s researchers attribute this decline to factors such as lower humidity and greater stability in the middle layers of the atmosphere – which also tends to be influenced by climate change and changing precipitation patterns, including longer droughts.

According to the study, losses caused by severe hail rose in the USA, Australia and Europe. This was largely attributable in Europe to the greater frequency of severe hailstorms and, indirectly, climate change; other factors played pivotal roles in Australia and the United States, including higher exposed values and/or greater vulnerability.

items.t: Andrew Fowles appointed Head of Broking at Munich Re Specialty – Binding Authorities
sum: Munich Re Specialty, a provider of specialty insurance solutions and part of the Munich Re Group, has appointed Andrew Fowles as Head of Broking within its Binding Authorities business.

Fowles has more than 25 years of experience in delegated authority and specialty underwriting, with a background spanning US property and casualty, Lloyd’s, and global excess and surplus lines markets.
He joins Munich Re Specialty from South Shore Insurance Underwriters (SSIU), where he held the role of Chief Underwriting Officer.
His previous experience includes senior leadership positions at Canopius Group as well as a number of Lloyd’s syndicates.
The appointment supports Munich Re Specialty – Binding Authorities’ continued focus on strengthening its broking capabilities and market presence.
